# Flood Depth vs. Flood Extent: Why Water Depth Matters for Better Disaster Decisions

**Published**: 2026-08-12  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/flood-depth-vs-flood-extent  
**Summary**: Flood extent shows where water went. Flood depth shows how severe it was — six inches in a parking lot vs six feet through a building. Why depth is the dimension that changes insurance, utility, and supply chain decisions.

**Flood maps can tell you where flooding occurred. Flood depth tells you how severe it was. For insurers, emergency managers, utilities, supply chain operators, and infrastructure owners, that difference can dramatically change operational decisions.**

_Banner: monsoon waters spreading across the Indus plains of Pakistan and northern India (NASA MODIS, August 9, 2026). A flood map shows one extent — but across that expanse, depth varies from inches to meters, and so do the consequences._

_This is Part 2 of a two-part series on flood intelligence. Part 1 —[Floods Are One of the World's Most Difficult Hazards to Measure](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/observed-flood-intelligence>) — covers how observed flood intelligence works._

## Flooding Isn't Binary

When organizations monitor flooding, the first question is usually: _"Did flooding occur?"_

Traditional flood alerts and inundation maps answer this question reasonably well. They identify rivers that have exceeded flood stage, areas under flood warnings, or geographic regions expected to experience flooding.

But that only tells part of the story.

A flooded parking lot and a neighborhood under eight feet of water may both appear as "flooded" on a map, yet they represent entirely different levels of risk, damage, and operational impact.

The more important question is: _"How deep is the water?"_

Flood depth transforms flood monitoring from simple situational awareness into actionable business intelligence.

## Why Flood Depth Is More Valuable Than Flood Extent

Knowing that an area flooded is useful. Knowing how deep the water became is significantly more valuable.

Water depth directly influences:

  * Expected property damage
  * Vehicle losses
  * Infrastructure impacts
  * Road accessibility
  * Utility disruptions
  * Agricultural losses
  * Business interruption
  * Insurance claims severity



For example, two commercial facilities may both lie inside a flood polygon. One experiences six inches of water in a loading area. The other experiences six feet of water throughout the building.

Traditional flood maps often treat both locations similarly. Flood depth reveals that the operational consequences are vastly different.

## Flood Depth Improves Decision Making

Organizations increasingly need more than alerts — they need context. Flood depth helps answer questions such as:

  * Which insured locations are likely to experience total losses?
  * Which substations may become inaccessible?
  * Which distribution centers should divert shipments?
  * Which roads remain passable?
  * Which communities require immediate response?
  * Which facilities can safely resume operations?



Instead of simply knowing that flooding occurred, decision makers gain insight into the likely consequences.

## The Challenge: Measuring Flood Depth in Real Time

Unlike temperature or rainfall, flood depth cannot be measured everywhere simultaneously. Different types of floods create different challenges:

  * **River flooding** follows channels where water levels can be measured.
  * **Flash floods** often develop rapidly in ungauged watersheds.
  * **Urban flooding** is influenced by storm drains, streets, and engineered infrastructure.
  * **Coastal flooding** combines tides, storm surge, waves, and rainfall.



No single sensor can observe flood depth across an entire landscape. As a result, flood intelligence relies on combining multiple authoritative observations and models.

See it live in DisasterAWARE

DisasterAWARE monitors 30+ hazard types worldwide in real time -- verified, impact-assessed, and ready to act on.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/?source=mid-article-cta&article=flood-depth-vs-flood-extent#start-your-free-trial-of-disasteraware-enterprise-now>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=flood-depth-vs-flood-extent>)

## From Observations to Flood Depth

Modern flood intelligence begins with observed conditions rather than assumptions.

As rivers rise above flood stage, authoritative gauge observations provide continuous measurements of water levels. These observations can be combined with official flood-inundation mapping and high-resolution terrain models to estimate flood depth across surrounding areas while the event is still unfolding.

As additional observations become available — including surveyed high-water marks and post-event measurements — the understanding of the event becomes even more accurate. Rather than relying on a single static product, flood intelligence evolves as new evidence arrives.

## Transparency Builds Trust

One of the biggest challenges in geospatial risk intelligence is understanding where information originates. Organizations need confidence that decisions are based on trusted data.

High-quality flood intelligence should clearly distinguish between:

  * Observed measurements
  * Modeled flood depth
  * Surveyed ground truth
  * Fused multi-source intelligence



Providing this transparency allows users to understand both the strengths and limitations of each dataset.

## How DisasterAWARE Approaches Flood Depth

DisasterAWARE combines multiple authoritative sources to deliver flood intelligence that evolves alongside the event itself — in the two phases described in [Part 1 of this series](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/observed-flood-intelligence>): near real-time operational intelligence during active flooding (flood severity, feet above flood stage, inundation extent, modeled depth, road and infrastructure impacts), and survey-grade ground truth afterward (measured flood depth surfaces from high-water marks and storm-tide measurements, suitable for damage assessment, claims analysis, and [historical event intelligence](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/historical-event-intelligence/>)).

## Applications Across Industries

**Insurance** — Prioritize claims response, estimate damage severity, assess portfolio exposure, improve catastrophe analytics, and trigger parametric payouts. (Full picture in [hazard data for insurers](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/hazard-data-for-insurers>).)

**Supply Chain** — Identify disrupted facilities, monitor transportation corridors, evaluate supplier impacts, and support business continuity.

**Utilities** — Monitor substations and critical infrastructure, assess accessibility for field crews, and prioritize restoration activities.

**Government & Emergency Management** — Improve situational awareness, allocate response resources, support recovery planning, and document historical impacts.

## The Future of Flood Intelligence

As climate-driven flooding becomes more frequent and more costly, organizations need more than warnings. They need to understand the actual severity of each event.

Flood depth provides that missing dimension. Rather than asking only _"Where did flooding occur?"_ , organizations can begin asking the more operationally meaningful question: _"How severe was the flooding, and what does it mean for the people, assets, and operations we care about?"_

That shift — from flood extent to flood depth — is helping organizations make faster, better-informed decisions before, during, and after flood events. Live flood events are on the [flood intelligence hub](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/current/floods>) now, and the data behind them is available through the [flood API](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/natural-disaster-api/>).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between flood depth and flood extent?** Flood extent shows _where_ water is — the footprint of a flood on a map. Flood depth shows _how much_ water is at each location. Two sites inside the same flood polygon can face completely different consequences: six inches in a parking lot versus six feet through a building.

**How is flood depth measured during an event?** No single sensor covers a landscape, so depth is derived by combining authoritative river-gauge observations with official flood-inundation mapping and high-resolution terrain models — then refined after the event with surveyed high-water marks and storm-tide measurements.

**Why does flood depth matter for insurance?** Depth is the strongest driver of loss severity: it separates minor claims from total losses, enables claims triage by likely damage, sharpens portfolio exposure estimates, and can support parametric triggers based on measured conditions.

# Floods Are One of the World's Most Difficult Hazards to Measure

**Published**: 2026-08-12  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/observed-flood-intelligence  
**Summary**: Forecasts predict where flooding may occur. Observed flood intelligence measures what actually happened — river stage, severity, inundation extent, and flood depth from authoritative federal observations, refined with survey-grade ground truth.

**Every year, floods cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage worldwide, disrupting communities, infrastructure, transportation, insurance portfolios, and supply chains. Yet despite decades of advances in forecasting and hydrologic modeling, one question remains surprisingly difficult to answer during an event: how deep is the water?**

_Banner: the lower Mississippi and its delta meeting the Gulf (NASA MODIS, August 10, 2026) — the most heavily gauged river system in America, where observation infrastructure turns flooding from guesswork into measurement._

Forecasts estimate where flooding may occur. Satellite imagery shows where water eventually appeared. But operational decisions require something different: organizations need to understand what is actually happening — not what might happen.

This is where observed flood intelligence becomes essential.

_This is Part 1 of a two-part series on flood intelligence. Part 2 —[Flood Depth vs. Flood Extent](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/flood-depth-vs-flood-extent>) — goes deeper on why water depth changes operational decisions._

## Moving Beyond Forecasts

Many flood monitoring systems focus primarily on forecasts. Forecast guidance is invaluable before an event, but once flooding begins, decision makers need to transition from prediction to observation.

DisasterAWARE was designed around this principle. Rather than relying solely on forecast models, the platform continuously incorporates authoritative observations from federal agencies to understand how flood events are actually unfolding — the same detect-verify-assess loop we described in [What Is Event Intelligence?](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/what-is-event-intelligence>), applied to the hazard that's hardest to measure.

This distinction matters for insurers, emergency managers, infrastructure operators, logistics providers, and organizations responsible for protecting people and assets.

## Two Phases of Flood Intelligence

Flood intelligence evolves as new observations become available. Rather than treating flood information as a single static dataset, DisasterAWARE delivers intelligence in two complementary phases.

### Phase One: Near Real-Time Operational Intelligence

Within minutes to hours after rivers begin exceeding flood stage, DisasterAWARE enriches flood events with:

  * Observed river stage
  * Flood severity
  * Feet above flood stage
  * Inundation extent
  * Modeled flood depth
  * Road impacts
  * Affected infrastructure and assets



This intelligence is derived from authoritative federal observations rather than forecast projections. Organizations gain situational awareness while response decisions are still being made.

### Phase Two: Survey-Grade Ground Truth

Major flood events continue to evolve long after waters recede. Federal survey teams later collect high-water marks, storm tide measurements, and surveyed water elevations.

DisasterAWARE incorporates these authoritative observations to produce measured flood depth surfaces representing actual flood conditions. Rather than replacing earlier intelligence, these observations refine it. Customers gain both immediate operational awareness and authoritative post-event analytics.

## Why Flood Depth Matters

Traditional flood alerts answer one question: will flooding occur?

Observed flood depth answers much more important questions:

  * Which facilities experienced six feet of flooding?
  * Which roads became impassable?
  * Which neighborhoods flooded most severely?
  * Which insured assets likely sustained catastrophic damage?
  * Which suppliers require immediate assistance?



Depth transforms flood monitoring into actionable business intelligence. (We explore this distinction fully in [Part 2 of this series](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/flood-depth-vs-flood-extent>).)

## Authoritative Data Instead of Black Boxes

One of the biggest challenges in flood analytics is trust. Organizations increasingly ask: where did this number come from?

DisasterAWARE emphasizes transparency. Flood intelligence is derived from authoritative federal observations, including:

  * USGS river gauges
  * NOAA water observations
  * National Weather Service flood intelligence
  * FEMA datasets
  * NASA surface-water observations where appropriate



Each flood product identifies the methodology supporting it. Customers know whether information represents observed measurements, modeled depth, measured depth, or fused intelligence.

## Designed for Enterprise Decision Making

Observed flood intelligence supports:

**Insurance** — Claims triage, portfolio monitoring, and catastrophe response. (See our full guide to [hazard data for insurers](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/hazard-data-for-insurers>).)

**Supply Chain** — Facility disruption, transportation impacts, supplier risk, and infrastructure protection.

**Utilities** — Substation monitoring and pipeline exposure.

**Financial Services** — Portfolio exposure, mortgage risk, and commercial real estate.

## Why Observed Intelligence Is Different

Forecasts estimate future conditions. Observed intelligence measures reality.

The combination of authoritative observations, flood depth, inundation extent, and operational impacts provides organizations with a far more complete understanding of flood events than alerts alone. Live flood events, tracked this way, are visible now on our [flood intelligence hub](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/current/floods>) — and available programmatically through the [flood API](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/natural-disaster-api/>).

As climate-driven flooding becomes increasingly frequent, observed intelligence is becoming an essential component of enterprise resilience.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is observed flood intelligence?** Observed flood intelligence measures what is actually happening during a flood — river stage from authoritative gauges, flood severity, inundation extent, and flood depth — rather than forecasting what might happen. It is derived from federal monitoring networks (USGS, NOAA, NWS, FEMA) and refined after major events with surveyed high-water marks.

**How is it different from a flood forecast?** Forecasts estimate future conditions before and early in an event. Observed intelligence takes over once flooding begins: actual measurements, updated as the event unfolds, then refined with survey-grade ground truth after waters recede.

**What are the two phases of flood intelligence?** Phase one is near real-time: within minutes to hours of rivers exceeding flood stage, events are enriched with observed stage, severity, extent, modeled depth, and impacts. Phase two is survey-grade: post-event high-water marks and storm-tide measurements produce measured flood depth surfaces for damage assessment and claims analysis.

# Verified Severe Convective Storm Intelligence: Why Historical Storm Reports Aren't Enough

**Published**: 2026-08-11  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/verified-severe-convective-storm-intelligence  
**Summary**: A warning doesn't mean severe weather occurred — warnings are forecasts. How each historic storm is reconstructed from observed evidence: verified hail, confirmed tornadoes with EF ratings, measured winds, complete provenance.

**Every year, thousands of severe storms occur. But surprisingly few are reconstructed into complete historical intelligence.**

_Banner: the storm system that produced the March 10, 2026 tornado outbreak — including the Wells County EF5 — as seen from space that day (NASA MODIS). From orbit it's one cloud mass; verified reconstruction is what turns it into tornado paths, hail swaths, and evidence._

A tornado touches down. Golf ball-sized hail damages thousands of roofs. Straight-line winds topple power poles across multiple counties. Emergency managers respond. Insurance claims are filed. Businesses recover.

Years later, organizations trying to understand what actually happened often discover that the historical record is fragmented. One database contains tornado reports. Another contains hail observations. Another contains radar products. Another contains warning polygons. Another contains damage surveys.

Each dataset tells only part of the story. The catastrophe itself has been scattered across dozens of disconnected records.

At DisasterAWARE, we believe historic disasters deserve better. That's why we've developed Verified Severe Convective Storm Intelligence as part of our [Historical Catastrophe Intelligence platform](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-catastrophe-intelligence>). Rather than archiving individual observations, we reconstruct complete severe storm events using authoritative observations from multiple trusted sources.

## The Hidden Problem with Historical Storm Data

For decades, historical severe weather datasets have focused on individual observations. One hail report. One tornado report. One wind observation. One warning. One radar product.

Each observation is valuable. None tells the complete story.

Imagine trying to understand Hurricane Katrina using only one wind measurement. Or reconstructing a wildfire from a single satellite image. The same problem exists with severe convective storms.

Storms evolve. They produce multiple hazards simultaneously. A single supercell may generate destructive hail, damaging straight-line winds, multiple tornadoes, extensive structural damage, dozens of Local Storm Reports, radar signatures, emergency warnings, and detailed damage surveys.

Those observations belong to one disaster. Historically, they have rarely been treated that way.

## What Defines a Severe Convective Storm?

Meteorologists generally define a severe thunderstorm as one capable of producing at least one of three hazards:

  * Hail at least one inch (2.54 cm) in diameter,
  * Wind gusts of 58 mph (50 knots) or greater,
  * Or a tornado.



Those thresholds are widely used operationally. But there's an important distinction. **Forecasts and warnings indicate that severe weather is possible or expected. Observed evidence tells us what actually happened.**

That distinction is critical for insurance, claims, risk analysis, historical research, and catastrophe intelligence.

## Forecasts Are Not Observations

One of the biggest misconceptions surrounding historical severe weather is assuming that a warning automatically means severe weather occurred.

It doesn't.

Warnings are forecasts. Some warned storms never produce severe weather. Other storms exceed expectations. For organizations making business decisions, the difference matters.

Did the storm actually produce one-inch hail? Was a tornado confirmed? Were damaging winds observed? Those answers should come from verified observations — not forecasts. (It's the same confirmed-versus-rumored discipline we described when [the Wells County EF5's rating](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/march-2026-tornado-outbreak-10-significant-tornadoes-ef5>) arrived from damage surveys days after social media had "confirmed" it.)

Evidence, not assumptions

Verified Severe Convective Storm records -- confirmed tornadoes, observed hail, measured winds, complete provenance -- ready for claims, underwriting, and exposure analysis.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/?source=mid-article-cta&article=verified-severe-convective-storm-intelligence#start-your-free-trial-of-disasteraware-enterprise-now>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=verified-severe-convective-storm-intelligence>)

## Reconstructing Verified Severe Convective Storms

DisasterAWARE approaches historical severe weather differently. Rather than storing isolated observations, we reconstruct each historic storm into a comprehensive intelligence record. Every event is evaluated using observed evidence from multiple authoritative sources, including:

  * National Weather Service Local Storm Reports
  * Storm Prediction Center reports
  * NWS Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT)
  * MRMS radar-derived hail swaths
  * Severe Thunderstorm and Tornado Warning polygons
  * Tornado damage surveys
  * Ground-based wind observations
  * Official storm narratives



Each observation is correlated spatially and temporally to build a complete picture of the event. The result is not simply a collection of reports. It is a reconstructed historic disaster.

## Verified Severe Convective Storm Classification

One of the newest capabilities within DisasterAWARE's Historical Catastrophe Intelligence platform is the reconstruction and classification of Verified Severe Convective Storms.

Rather than assuming every warned storm was severe, every reconstructed event is evaluated against observed evidence. DisasterAWARE determines whether an event qualifies as a Severe Convective Storm by confirming that one or more established severe weather thresholds were actually observed.

For each reconstructed storm, the platform identifies:

  * Whether tornadoes occurred
  * The highest EF rating
  * Maximum observed hail size
  * Maximum observed wind speed
  * The severe hazards that were present
  * The evidence supporting each determination



Every classification includes complete provenance, allowing analysts to understand not only the outcome, but also the observations used to reach that conclusion. This creates a transparent, repeatable methodology for identifying verified severe storms rather than relying solely on warnings or forecasts.

## More Than Tornadoes

Severe Convective Storms are multi-peril events. DisasterAWARE captures the complete hazard picture. Each reconstructed event may include:

**Tornado Intelligence** — Touchdown paths, EF ratings, damage path geometries, survey points and narratives, and casualty information where available.

**Hail Intelligence** — Measured and estimated hail reports, radar-derived MRMS hail swaths, maximum hail size, and insurance-oriented hail classifications.

**Wind Intelligence** — Measured and estimated gusts, wind damage reports, storm narratives, and warning tags.

**Operational Intelligence** — Warning polygons, Local Storm Reports, SPC reports, event timelines, and supporting evidence.

Instead of asking whether a tornado occurred nearby, organizations gain a complete operational history of the storm. (Live severe weather is on the [tornado intelligence hub](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/current/tornadoes>) right now — and every event tracked there becomes part of tomorrow's verified historical record.)

## Why This Matters for Insurance

Severe Convective Storms are among the costliest catastrophe perils for insurers. But accurately reconstructing historical storms has traditionally required analysts to manually compare multiple datasets. Verified Severe Convective Storm Intelligence dramatically simplifies that process:

  * **Claims teams** can determine whether severe weather was actually observed.
  * **Underwriters** can understand the historical catastrophe profile of a property.
  * **Exposure analysts** can evaluate portfolio impacts using verified event footprints rather than isolated reports.
  * **Risk managers** can investigate recurring patterns of hail, wind, and tornado activity across portfolios.



Historical catastrophe intelligence becomes directly usable — not merely archival. (The broader insurance picture is in [hazard data for insurers](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/hazard-data-for-insurers>).)

## Built on Observations. Enhanced with Intelligence.

DisasterAWARE doesn't replace authoritative weather data. We build upon it. Every reconstructed Severe Convective Storm begins with trusted observations from organizations such as the National Weather Service and Storm Prediction Center. Those observations are then verified, correlated, enriched, classified, and published as a single historical intelligence record.

The result is a richer understanding of how historic disasters actually unfolded.

## Historical Catastrophe Intelligence Changes the Question

Traditional historical storm databases encourage users to ask: _was there a tornado report?_

Historical Catastrophe Intelligence asks: _what historic disaster occurred here — and what verified evidence tells its complete story?_

That's a fundamentally different question. And it produces fundamentally better intelligence. Because organizations don't make decisions based on isolated observations. They make decisions based on understanding the complete catastrophe.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does a severe thunderstorm warning mean severe weather occurred?** No. Warnings are forecasts — statements that severe weather is possible or expected. Some warned storms never produce severe conditions; others exceed expectations. Whether severe weather _occurred_ is established by observed evidence: measured hail, confirmed tornadoes, verified wind gusts, and damage surveys.

**What officially qualifies as a severe thunderstorm?** A storm producing at least one of: hail one inch (2.54 cm) or larger in diameter, wind gusts of 58 mph (50 knots) or greater, or a tornado. DisasterAWARE classifies a storm as a Verified Severe Convective Storm only when observed evidence confirms at least one threshold was actually met.

**How are tornadoes confirmed?** By National Weather Service damage surveys — teams assess the damage path and assign an EF rating after the event, sometimes days later. Verified storm records carry the confirmed touchdown paths, EF ratings, survey points, and narratives, with full provenance for each determination.

**Why do insurers need verified storm data instead of warnings?** Claims and underwriting decisions turn on what happened at a location, not what was forecast: whether one-inch hail was actually observed, whether a tornado was confirmed, what wind speeds were measured. Verified event footprints replace the manual cross-referencing of tornado databases, hail reports, radar archives, and survey records.

# Historical Catastrophe Intelligence and Catastrophe Models: Why Better Models Begin with Better Historical Intelligence

**Published**: 2026-08-11  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-catastrophe-intelligence-vs-catastrophe-models  
**Summary**: Catastrophe models simulate what could happen. Historical Catastrophe Intelligence reconstructs what actually happened. One predicts; the other documents — and every model ultimately depends on the quality of the historical record beneath it.

## Two Different Questions. Two Different Types of Intelligence.

**For decades, catastrophe models have been indispensable tools for insurers, reinsurers, banks, governments, and large enterprises.** They help organizations answer an essential question: _what could happen?_

_Banner: all 1,702 historic tropical cyclones reconstructed in DisasterAWARE's enhancement pipeline, drawn from IBTrACS best-track data and colored by intensity — from tropical storm (blue) to Category 5 (deep red). This is the observed record that catastrophe models are built on._

By simulating thousands — or even millions — of plausible disaster scenarios, catastrophe models estimate the probability and financial impact of future hurricanes, earthquakes, floods, severe convective storms, wildfires, and other perils. These probabilistic models combine hazard science, engineering, exposure data, and financial modeling to support underwriting, capital allocation, portfolio management, and regulatory reporting.

But there is another question that organizations increasingly need to answer: _what actually happened?_

That is a fundamentally different problem. And it requires a fundamentally different kind of intelligence.

## Prediction and Reconstruction Serve Different Purposes

Historical Catastrophe Intelligence is not a catastrophe model. Nor is it intended to replace one.

Catastrophe models simulate plausible future events. Historical Catastrophe Intelligence reconstructs verified historic disasters. One predicts. The other documents. One estimates probabilities. The other establishes facts.

Both are essential. In fact, they become even more valuable when used together.

## Catastrophe Models Begin with History

Every catastrophe model ultimately depends on history. Historical hurricanes. Historical earthquakes. Historical floods. Historical severe storms. Historical wildfire activity.

Historical observations help scientists understand hazard frequency, severity, behavior, and spatial variability before generating thousands of synthetic events. Industry guidance continues to emphasize the importance of high-quality historical hazard data as a foundation for catastrophe modeling — the stochastic event catalog at the heart of every model is seeded, calibrated, and validated against the observed record.

But history itself has traditionally been fragmented.

## The Challenge with Historical Disaster Records

Most historical catastrophe records were never designed to become enterprise intelligence. Instead, they exist as separate collections of observations.

A severe storm might include tornado reports, hail reports, radar products, warning polygons, wind observations, damage surveys, and emergency narratives. Each dataset serves an important purpose. Yet none tells the complete story. The catastrophe itself becomes fragmented across dozens of independent sources.

Organizations must manually assemble the puzzle.

The observed record, enterprise-ready

Verified historical disasters -- reconstructed event by event -- for model validation, claims analysis, and exposure work. Built on authoritative observations.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/?source=mid-article-cta&article=historical-catastrophe-intelligence-vs-catastrophe-models#start-your-free-trial-of-disasteraware-enterprise-now>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=historical-catastrophe-intelligence-vs-catastrophe-models>)

## Historical Catastrophe Intelligence Reconstructs the Event

DisasterAWARE approaches historical disasters differently. Instead of preserving isolated observations, we reconstruct complete catastrophe events. Authoritative observations from government agencies are collected, verified, correlated, enriched, and published as enterprise-ready intelligence. (The full methodology is in [Historical Catastrophe Intelligence, explained](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-catastrophe-intelligence>).)

Every reconstructed event captures not simply that a disaster occurred — but how it evolved. For example:

**A historic hurricane becomes:** advisory-by-advisory tracks, wind radii, landfalls, pressure evolution, storm intensity, and hurricane-force duration.

**A historic wildfire becomes:** fire progression, smoke evolution, air quality impacts, evacuation zones, and operational timelines.

**A historic earthquake becomes:** ground shaking intensity, Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA), Modified Mercalli Intensity, and shaking contours.

**A historic Severe Convective Storm becomes:** verified hail observations, radar-derived hail swaths, tornado touchdown paths, EF ratings, wind observations, damage survey information, and an evidence-based [Verified Severe Convective Storm classification](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/verified-severe-convective-storm-intelligence>).

The result is not simply historical weather. It is Historical Catastrophe Intelligence.

## Why Historical Intelligence Makes Better Models

Historical Catastrophe Intelligence creates opportunities throughout the catastrophe modeling lifecycle.

**Better Hazard Characterization** — Reconstructed disasters provide richer representations of actual historical events than isolated observations alone. Instead of relying on individual reports, analysts gain a complete understanding of how each catastrophe evolved.

**Better Validation** — Historical Catastrophe Intelligence provides a richer benchmark for comparing simulated events against real-world catastrophes. Rather than validating against a single observation, analysts can compare modeled behavior with reconstructed event evolution.

**Better Exposure Analysis** — Historical intelligence allows organizations to evaluate which facilities were affected, which suppliers were disrupted, which insured properties experienced verified hazards, and how operational impacts unfolded. This complements — not replaces — the probabilistic view provided by catastrophe models.

**Better Claims Analysis** — Following a disaster, organizations often need to answer questions that catastrophe models were never intended to answer: Was hail actually observed at this location? Did this property experience verified hurricane-force winds? Was there a confirmed tornado? Were evacuation orders issued? How did the wildfire evolve over time? Historical Catastrophe Intelligence provides the event-level evidence needed to answer those questions.

## Simulation Meets Observation

Think of catastrophe models and Historical Catastrophe Intelligence as two complementary lenses. Organizations need both. One informs future risk. The other explains historical reality.

## Historical Intelligence Is Becoming More Important

Organizations today face increasing scrutiny from regulators, investors, and customers. They are expected to understand historical portfolio exposure, operational resilience, physical climate risk, infrastructure vulnerability, disaster response, and claims performance.

Historical Catastrophe Intelligence provides the factual foundation for those analyses. Rather than relying on disconnected observations, organizations gain verified historical records that describe disasters as they actually unfolded. (For how this fits the broader insurance data stack — including underwriting in markets where no commercial cat model exists — see [hazard data for insurers](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/hazard-data-for-insurers>).)

## Built on Authoritative Observations

DisasterAWARE reconstructs historic disasters using authoritative information from organizations such as NOAA, the National Weather Service, the Storm Prediction Center, USGS, NASA, IBTrACS, MRMS, FEMA, and federal, state, provincial, and local emergency agencies.

We don't replace authoritative science. We organize it. We verify it. We enrich it. We connect it. We transform it into enterprise-ready Historical Catastrophe Intelligence — available today through [Historical Event Intelligence](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/historical-event-intelligence/>).

## The Future Is Not Models or Intelligence. It Is Both.

The future of catastrophe risk management will not be built on a single dataset or a single model. Organizations will increasingly combine catastrophe models, historical catastrophe intelligence, [real-time event intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/what-is-event-intelligence>), climate intelligence, exposure analytics, and operational risk monitoring.

Together, these capabilities provide a more complete understanding of both future uncertainty and historical reality.

Catastrophe models help answer what could happen next. Historical Catastrophe Intelligence helps explain what actually happened.

The strongest decisions come from understanding both.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between a catastrophe model and historical catastrophe intelligence?** A catastrophe model simulates thousands of plausible future events (a stochastic event set) to estimate probability and financial impact. Historical catastrophe intelligence reconstructs verified past events as they actually occurred. One predicts; the other documents. Models are built and validated using the historical record.

**Can historical catastrophe intelligence replace a catastrophe model?** No — and it isn't meant to. The two are complementary: models quantify future uncertainty; the observed record establishes facts, validates model behavior, supports claims analysis, and provides a defensible baseline in regions or perils where commercial models don't exist.

**How does the observed record improve catastrophe model validation?** Instead of validating a simulated event against one or two isolated reports, analysts can compare modeled behavior against a fully reconstructed event — a hurricane's advisory-by-advisory intensity and wind field, or a storm's verified hail swath and tornado paths — a far richer benchmark.

**What is a historical event catalog?** The record of what has actually happened — the observed complement to the stochastic (synthetic) event catalogs inside catastrophe models. Stochastic catalogs are built from historical catalogs plus physical science and statistics, which makes the quality and completeness of the historical record foundational to every model built on it.

# Historical Catastrophe Intelligence: Rebuilding Historic Disasters into Verified Enterprise Intelligence

**Published**: 2026-08-11  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-catastrophe-intelligence  
**Summary**: Historical weather records what the atmosphere did. Historical Catastrophe Intelligence reconstructs what actually happened — hurricanes advisory by advisory, storms with verified evidence, wildfires as they spread — rebuilt, verified, and published.

## The Problem with Historical Weather Data

**Every organization relies on history to make better decisions.** Insurance companies analyze past catastrophes to understand losses and improve underwriting. Supply chain teams investigate historical disruptions to strengthen resilience. Governments study previous disasters to improve emergency planning. Businesses evaluate historic events to guide investments, continuity planning, and climate adaptation.

_Banner: Typhoon Dolphin approaching Japan's southern islands, August 6, 2026 (NASA satellite imagery). Every advisory, wind field, and landfall of this storm is now a permanently reconstructed record in DisasterAWARE — history, preserved as it happened._

Yet despite the abundance of historical weather data, many organizations still struggle to answer a surprisingly simple question: **what actually happened?**

Traditional weather archives tell us how the atmosphere behaved. They record rainfall totals, wind speeds, temperatures, radar imagery, and satellite observations. These datasets are invaluable for forecasting, climatology, and scientific research.

But enterprise decision-makers are rarely asking about the weather itself. Instead, they ask questions like:

  * Which catastrophe impacted this facility?
  * How did the event evolve over time?
  * What hazards were actually observed?
  * Which assets were exposed?
  * How severe was the event?
  * What operational impacts occurred?
  * How does this compare with previous disasters?



Those questions require far more than historical weather observations. They require Historical Catastrophe Intelligence.

## From Historical Weather to Historical Intelligence

There is an important distinction between historical weather and historical catastrophe intelligence. **Historical weather tells us what the atmosphere was doing. Historical catastrophe intelligence reconstructs what actually happened.**

Every disaster generates thousands — or even millions — of observations from satellites, radar systems, weather stations, emergency agencies, field surveys, and scientific instruments. Individually, these observations provide only fragments of the story. Together, they reveal the complete lifecycle of a catastrophe.

At DisasterAWARE, we've spent years developing technologies that rebuild historic disasters from authoritative observations, transforming disconnected datasets into rich, verified intelligence records. Rather than publishing isolated weather measurements, we reconstruct catastrophes as complete operational events.

## Rebuilding Historic Disasters

Every catastrophe leaves behind evidence. Satellite imagery. Radar scans. Government warnings. Damage surveys. Ground reports. Fire perimeters. River gauges. Earthquake shaking measurements. Smoke plumes. Emergency evacuations.

The challenge isn't finding data. The challenge is connecting it.

DisasterAWARE's Historical Catastrophe Intelligence platform continuously integrates authoritative information from trusted government agencies and scientific organizations, correlates related observations, validates conflicting information, enriches each event with additional intelligence, and publishes complete historical disaster records for enterprise use.

Every historical catastrophe follows the same methodology:

**Rebuilt** — Authoritative observations are collected from trusted government agencies and scientific organizations around the world.

**Verified** — Observations are validated, reconciled, and correlated into coherent disaster events.

**Enriched** — Additional analytics, geometries, assessments, classifications, and operational intelligence are added to each event.

**Published** — The completed catastrophe becomes an enterprise-ready intelligence record available through DisasterAWARE APIs, GIS services, dashboards, and analytics platforms.

The result is a continuously growing library of reconstructed historic disasters rather than disconnected historical datasets.

## Every Historic Disaster Tells a Story

Disasters evolve. A hurricane strengthens, weakens, changes direction, and makes multiple landfalls. A tornado-producing storm generates hail, damaging winds, warnings, and multiple tornado touchdowns. A wildfire expands, produces smoke, triggers evacuations, and affects air quality hundreds of miles away. An earthquake creates dramatically different shaking intensities across a region despite originating from a single epicenter.

Historical Catastrophe Intelligence captures those stories. Instead of preserving only that an event occurred, DisasterAWARE preserves how it unfolded. (We watched this play out in real time with [Typhoon Dolphin's double landfall](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/typhoon-dolphin-2026-okinawa-china-double-landfall>) — every advisory of which is now part of the storm's permanent reconstructed record.)

## Reconstructing Every Historic Hurricane

Tropical cyclones are among the most complex natural hazards on Earth. A simple track line tells only a fraction of the story.

DisasterAWARE enriches historical cyclones using authoritative information from NOAA's International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS), rebuilding every storm into a comprehensive operational record. Each reconstructed hurricane includes:

  * Complete advisory tracks (A-deck and B-deck)
  * Advisory-by-advisory positions
  * Wind radii (34-, 50-, and 64-knot winds by quadrant)
  * Maximum sustained winds and minimum central pressure
  * Saffir-Simpson category
  * Hurricane-force and major-hurricane-force duration
  * Landfall history
  * Storm evolution over time and distance to land



Rather than seeing where a hurricane traveled, organizations gain a complete understanding of how the storm evolved throughout its lifecycle.

## Rebuilding Verified Severe Convective Storms

Severe Convective Storms (SCS) represent one of the largest sources of insured catastrophe losses globally. Yet they have historically been some of the most difficult events to reconstruct accurately.

Traditional historical datasets often contain isolated pieces of information — tornado reports, hail reports, wind observations, radar products, warning polygons, damage surveys — rarely connected into a single verified event.

DisasterAWARE changes that. Our platform reconstructs each historic storm by combining authoritative observations from the National Weather Service, Storm Prediction Center, MRMS radar, Local Storm Reports, tornado damage surveys, and other trusted sources.

More importantly, every event is evaluated to determine whether it truly qualifies as a **Verified Severe Convective Storm**. Unlike systems that rely solely on forecasts or warning issuance, DisasterAWARE classifies storms using observed evidence: a storm qualifies only when verified observations demonstrate that accepted thresholds have been met.

Each reconstructed event includes tornado touchdown paths, EF ratings, damage paths, survey points and narratives, measured and estimated hail reports, radar-derived hail swaths, wind observations, storm damage reports, warning polygons, the Severe Convective Storm classification, and complete evidence provenance. (The full methodology is in our companion piece on [Verified Severe Convective Storm Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/verified-severe-convective-storm-intelligence>).)

## Reconstructing Historic Wildfires

Wildfires are dynamic events. They ignite. They spread. They merge. They produce smoke. They trigger evacuations. They degrade air quality across entire regions. Traditional wildfire archives often preserve only snapshots in time.

Historical Catastrophe Intelligence preserves the complete operational evolution of each wildfire: fire progression and growth, incident evolution, smoke plume geometries, smoke forecasts and observations, air quality measurements, evacuation zones, operational incident information, and burn perimeters.

Organizations can replay how a wildfire unfolded — not simply where it burned. (How those incidents get built in the first place: [our wildfire intelligence overview](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/wildfire-intelligence-beyond-satellite-hotspots>).)

## Understanding Earthquakes Beyond Magnitude

Magnitude is only one measure of an earthquake. Damage depends on ground shaking.

Using authoritative USGS ShakeMap data, DisasterAWARE reconstructs earthquakes with detailed shaking intelligence, including Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA), Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI), shaking contour geometries, ground-motion polygons, earthquake metadata, and event assessments.

This enables organizations to understand not simply where an earthquake occurred, but how strongly different locations were affected.

## Reconstructing Historic Floods

Flooding is one of the most expensive and widespread natural hazards, yet it has historically been difficult to reconstruct accurately.

DisasterAWARE is expanding its capabilities to include detailed flood reconstruction using observed flood extents, water depths, authoritative gauge information, and satellite-derived inundation mapping. Rather than identifying where flooding was possible, organizations will be able to understand where flooding actually occurred, how deep it became, and how conditions evolved over time — the same [observed flood intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/observed-flood-intelligence>) approach we apply to live events, extended backward through history.

## Why Historical Catastrophe Intelligence Matters

Rich historical intelligence transforms how organizations analyze risk:

  * **Insurance carriers** can validate claims against verified catastrophe footprints.
  * **Underwriters** can better understand historical hazard exposure.
  * **Supply chain teams** can investigate previous disruptions.
  * **Business continuity leaders** can evaluate operational impacts.
  * **Governments** can improve disaster planning.
  * **Researchers** can study the complete evolution of historic disasters.



Instead of asking what the weather was, organizations can ask what actually happened. (For the insurance-specific picture — including how the observed record seeds and validates catastrophe models — see [hazard data for insurers](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/hazard-data-for-insurers>).)

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is historical catastrophe intelligence?** The reconstruction of past disasters as complete, verified events — rather than scattered observations. Authoritative data from agencies like NOAA, NWS, USGS, and FEMA is collected, correlated, validated, enriched with analytics and geometries, and published as enterprise-ready records of how each catastrophe actually unfolded.

**How is it different from historical weather data?** Historical weather records what the atmosphere did — rainfall, wind, temperature. Historical catastrophe intelligence reconstructs the _event_ : which disaster occurred, how it evolved, what hazards were verified, what was exposed, and how severe it was at each location.

**What hazard types are reconstructed?** Hurricanes (advisory-by-advisory from IBTrACS, with wind radii and landfall history), severe convective storms (verified tornado, hail, and wind evidence), wildfires (progression, smoke, evacuations, perimeters), and earthquakes (ShakeMap-based shaking intensity). Detailed flood reconstruction is being added.

**Who uses historical catastrophe intelligence?** Insurance claims and underwriting teams, catastrophe modelers validating against observed events, supply chain and business continuity analysts, government planners, and researchers studying how disasters actually unfold.

# How DisasterAWARE Enhances NASA FIRMS for Enterprise Wildfire Intelligence

**Published**: 2026-08-11  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/nasa-firms-enterprise-wildfire-intelligence  
**Summary**: NASA FIRMS is one of the world's most respected wildfire detection sources — and DisasterAWARE builds on it. How satellite observations become enterprise intelligence: incidents, official context, and connection to your assets.

**NASA FIRMS is an exceptional foundation. Enterprise decision-making requires more.**

_Banner: NASA FIRMS in action — Pacific Northwest fires on August 10, 2026, with each red VIIRS thermal detection overlaid on the smoke it explains. The detections are the start of the story, not the end._

When organizations begin evaluating wildfire intelligence solutions, one of the first resources they encounter is NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). For good reason.

NASA FIRMS is one of the world's most respected sources of near real-time wildfire detection, providing satellite-derived active fire observations from MODIS and VIIRS instruments. It has become an indispensable resource for emergency managers, researchers, governments, humanitarian organizations, and commercial users worldwide. FIRMS delivers global coverage, frequent updates, APIs, web services, downloadable datasets, and alerting capabilities that make it one of the foundational datasets for wildfire monitoring.

At DisasterAWARE, we rely on NASA FIRMS as one of several authoritative inputs into our wildfire intelligence platform. But enterprise customers aren't simply looking for wildfire detections. They're trying to answer operational questions:

  * Are any of my facilities threatened?
  * Which suppliers are impacted?
  * Is this a new wildfire or an existing incident?
  * Is the fire growing?
  * Should we notify our operations team?
  * Which insured assets require immediate attention?



Those questions require intelligence — not simply satellite observations.

## NASA FIRMS Answers "Where Is Heat Being Detected?"

NASA FIRMS excels at rapidly identifying thermal anomalies observed by satellites. Its strengths include near real-time satellite detections, global geographic coverage, MODIS and VIIRS observations, APIs and web services, email alerting, historical fire archives, and frequent data updates.

This makes FIRMS one of the earliest indicators that wildfire activity may be occurring. However, thermal anomalies are observations — not incidents. One wildfire can generate hundreds or thousands of individual detections over its lifetime.

## Enterprise Operations Need Incidents, Not Thousands of Hotspots

Imagine monitoring a major wildfire using only raw satellite detections. Every satellite overpass may identify dozens or hundreds of new hotspots. Some overlap previous detections. Others represent new fire growth. Some may disappear because of cloud cover or viewing geometry.

Without additional processing, operations teams quickly face information overload.

Rather than asking _"Where are the hotspots?"_ , enterprise users ask _"Which wildfire is threatening my business?"_ Those are fundamentally different questions.

## DisasterAWARE Transforms Satellite Observations into Wildfire Intelligence

DisasterAWARE doesn't replace NASA FIRMS. It builds upon it.

Our proprietary wildfire intelligence engine continuously ingests satellite observations and transforms them into operationally meaningful wildfire incidents. Instead of displaying disconnected thermal detections, our analytics:

  * Correlate related observations across space and time
  * Cluster multiple detections into a single wildfire incident
  * Reduce duplicate observations
  * Identify newly emerging fires
  * Continuously update incident footprints
  * Enrich incidents with operational metadata
  * Support exposure analysis and alerting



The result is a cleaner operational picture that aligns with how organizations actually monitor wildfire risk.

FIRMS speed, enterprise context

DisasterAWARE transforms NASA FIRMS detections into verified incidents connected to your facilities, suppliers, and insured assets.

## Authoritative Sources Strengthen Situational Awareness

Satellite observations are only one part of wildfire intelligence. Official incident management organizations provide another. To deliver a more complete operational picture, DisasterAWARE now integrates information from the U.S. National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC), Canadian wildfire authorities, Australian wildfire authorities, and European wildfire authorities, alongside NASA FIRMS.

This additional context includes official incident names, incident status, operational updates, wildfire metadata, and authoritative reporting.

Interestingly, NASA itself points users to NIFC and the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre (CIFFC) as complementary operational wildfire resources, reinforcing that satellite observations and incident management data serve different — but complementary — purposes.

Rather than forcing organizations to compare multiple government websites and datasets, DisasterAWARE brings these sources together into a unified operational view.

## Intelligence Doesn't End with Detection

Knowing a wildfire exists is valuable. Knowing how it affects your organization is where business value is created.

DisasterAWARE connects wildfire intelligence directly with customer assets, including facilities, offices, warehouses, suppliers, critical infrastructure, transportation networks, insured properties, employees, and customers.

Instead of manually comparing wildfire maps with spreadsheets of locations, organizations immediately understand what is exposed and where action may be required.

## Purpose-Built for Enterprise Workflows

Wildfire intelligence supports very different decisions depending on the organization:

**Insurance** — Portfolio exposure, claims triage and event response, event monitoring, risk accumulation, and parametric trigger payouts. (See [hazard data for insurers](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/hazard-data-for-insurers>).)

**Supply Chain** — Supplier disruption, transportation impacts, manufacturing interruptions, and logistics planning.

**Corporate Security & Business Continuity** — Employee safety, office closures, facility monitoring, and crisis response.

**Government & Humanitarian Organizations** — Situational awareness, resource prioritization, emergency coordination, and community impact assessment.

Each of these use cases requires much more than a map of satellite hotspots. They require actionable intelligence.

## A Layered Approach to Wildfire Intelligence

At DisasterAWARE, we think about wildfire intelligence as [four connected layers](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/wildfire-detection-to-decision>): **detection** (satellite observations, as fast as possible), **verification** (official agencies confirm and name incidents), **intelligence** (proprietary models organize and continuously enrich incidents), and **impact** (exposure assessment against the assets that matter to you).

This layered approach enables organizations to move beyond simply seeing fires toward understanding their operational significance.

## Why It Matters

NASA FIRMS has fundamentally changed how the world monitors wildfire activity. It remains one of the most valuable publicly available wildfire resources, and DisasterAWARE is proud to incorporate it into our intelligence platform.

But enterprise decision-makers need more than detections. They need trusted intelligence that combines the speed of satellite observations, the authority of official incident reporting, proprietary analytics, and direct business context — see it live on the [wildfire intelligence hub](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/current/wildfires>), or through the [wildfire API](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/natural-disaster-api/>).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is NASA FIRMS free to use?** Yes — FIRMS is an open, publicly available NASA resource offering near real-time fire detections, APIs, web services, downloadable data, and email alerts. DisasterAWARE incorporates it as one of several authoritative inputs and adds incident clustering, official agency context, and exposure analysis on top.

**What's the difference between FIRMS hotspots and DisasterAWARE wildfire incidents?** A FIRMS hotspot is a single thermal observation from one satellite pass. A DisasterAWARE incident is the operational event those observations belong to: correlated across passes and sensors, deduplicated, tracked as it grows, enriched with official incident names and status, and scored for exposed assets.

**Does DisasterAWARE compete with NASA FIRMS?** No — it builds on it. NASA's own documentation points users toward operational incident agencies like NIFC and CIFFC as complementary resources; DisasterAWARE fuses those layers (and more) into one enterprise picture, with FIRMS as a foundational detection input.

# Why No Single Wildfire Data Source Tells the Whole Story

**Published**: 2026-08-11  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/wildfire-data-sources-complete-picture  
**Summary**: Every wildfire dataset has strengths and limitations — and a single source fails exactly when accuracy matters most. Satellites deliver speed; agencies deliver context; analytics connect everything.

**Every wildfire dataset has strengths. Every wildfire dataset has limitations. Organizations that rely on a single source often discover these limitations during the moments when accurate information matters most.**

_Banner: smoke and haze veiling the Aegean from Greece to Türkiye (NASA MODIS, August 10, 2026) — from any single vantage point, you can't tell where it came from or what's still burning. That's why one data source is never enough._

The reality is simple: no single wildfire data source provides a complete operational picture.

## Satellites Deliver Speed

Satellite observations, including NASA FIRMS, provide some of the fastest indications that a wildfire may be burning. Within hours of satellite overpasses, thermal anomalies can identify potential fire activity across nearly every continent.

That speed is invaluable.

But satellites don't know incident names. They don't report containment. They don't coordinate emergency response.

## Incident Agencies Deliver Operational Context

In the United States, the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) coordinates national wildfire information across multiple federal agencies. Canada's wildfire organizations provide similar operational reporting for incidents across Canadian provinces. NASA FIRMS itself points users to NIFC and the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre (CIFFC) as complementary operational resources.

These organizations contribute critical information such as:

  * Official incident names
  * Fire status
  * Operational updates
  * Response information



One operational picture

DisasterAWARE fuses satellite detection, official incident reporting, and proprietary analytics into complementary intelligence -- not competing datasets.

## Analytics Connect Everything Together

This is where DisasterAWARE adds value. Rather than choosing one source, our platform fuses multiple authoritative datasets with proprietary analytics.

The result is a richer understanding of wildfire activity that combines:

  * Satellite detection
  * Official incident reporting
  * Fire clustering
  * Geospatial analytics
  * Exposure intelligence



Each source strengthens the others. Instead of competing datasets, organizations receive complementary intelligence.

## Better Decisions Begin with Better Context

Whether you're protecting employees, underwriting insurance, or managing global operations, the question isn't _"Which wildfire dataset should I trust?"_

The better question is: _"How can I combine the best available information into one operational picture?"_

That's exactly the philosophy behind [DisasterAWARE's wildfire intelligence platform](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/wildfire-intelligence-beyond-satellite-hotspots>) — and you can see the combined picture live on the [wildfire hub](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/current/wildfires>).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What are the main sources of wildfire data?** Three complementary families: satellite thermal detection (NASA FIRMS via MODIS and VIIRS — fast, global), official incident reporting (NIFC in the US, CIFFC in Canada, and counterpart agencies internationally — names, status, containment), and analytic layers that cluster detections into incidents and assess exposure.

**Why do satellites and incident agencies disagree about a fire?** They measure different things on different clocks: a satellite reports heat observed at overpass time; an agency reports the operationally confirmed incident. Early in a fire, satellites often lead; later, agency perimeters and containment status are the authoritative record. Fusing both gives speed and truth.

**Does DisasterAWARE replace government wildfire data?** No — it builds on it. Authoritative sources are the inputs; the platform's value is correlating, deduplicating, and enriching them into one continuously updated operational picture connected to your assets.

# Why Satellite Fire Detections Alone Aren't Enough

**Published**: 2026-08-11  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/satellite-fire-detections-vs-wildfire-intelligence  
**Summary**: A satellite can identify thousands of thermal anomalies from one wildfire — but not which fire it is, whether it's growing, or what it threatens. Why detection and intelligence are fundamentally different questions.

**Nearly every wildfire intelligence platform today starts with satellite observations.** NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) has become one of the world's most trusted sources for detecting active fires using thermal observations from MODIS and VIIRS satellites, delivering near real-time fire detections across the globe.

_Banner: British Columbia's fire complexes (NASA imagery, August 10, 2026) — every red point is one VIIRS thermal detection; the haze is smoke. Thousands of points, a handful of actual fires: the difference between data and intelligence._

These observations are incredibly valuable. They tell us where heat has been detected.

But that's not the same thing as understanding a wildfire.

## The Difference Between Data and Intelligence

Imagine looking at a city from an airplane at night. You can see thousands of lights. But you don't know which lights belong to hospitals, airports, schools, factories, or homes.

Raw wildfire detections work much the same way.

A satellite may identify hundreds — or thousands — of thermal anomalies associated with a single wildfire. Additional detections arrive as satellites make new passes. Smoke, clouds, terrain, and viewing angles all influence what satellites observe.

While this information is essential, it rarely answers the questions organizations actually need answered:

  * Which fire is this?
  * Is it growing?
  * How large is it?
  * Is it threatening my facilities?
  * Is it officially recognized by incident managers?
  * Should my operations team take action?



Those are intelligence questions — not detection questions.

From hotspots to incidents

DisasterAWARE transforms raw satellite detections into coherent, continuously updated wildfire incidents -- with the exposure context that makes them actionable.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/?source=mid-article-cta&article=satellite-fire-detections-vs-wildfire-intelligence#start-your-free-trial-of-disasteraware-enterprise-now>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=satellite-fire-detections-vs-wildfire-intelligence>)

## The Enterprise Challenge

Organizations responsible for protecting people, infrastructure, supply chains, or insured assets don't have time to interpret thousands of satellite detections. They need a continuously updated operational picture.

That's why DisasterAWARE transforms raw satellite observations into coherent wildfire incidents. Rather than presenting thousands of individual hotspots, our proprietary models correlate related detections over time and space, reducing noise and organizing observations into meaningful wildfire events.

The result is a cleaner operational picture that's easier to monitor, analyze, and act upon — you can see it running now on the [live wildfire hub](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/current/wildfires>).

## Intelligence Requires Context

Satellite detections remain one of the most important inputs into wildfire monitoring. But they're only one piece of the puzzle. Operational decision-making also requires:

  * Authoritative incident information
  * Fire growth analysis
  * Exposure assessments
  * Historical context
  * Geospatial analytics



The future of wildfire intelligence isn't about choosing one data source. It's about intelligently combining many of them into a single operational view — the full architecture is in our [wildfire intelligence overview](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/wildfire-intelligence-beyond-satellite-hotspots>).

That is the difference between seeing fires — and understanding them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does one wildfire generate thousands of satellite detections?** Each satellite pass records every thermal anomaly it observes — and a large fire burns for days across a wide area, observed by multiple satellites at different times and angles. Without clustering and deduplication, those observations accumulate into thousands of overlapping points for a single incident.

**Can satellite detections show a fire's perimeter or containment?** No. Thermal detections indicate where heat was observed — they don't define perimeters, report containment status, or carry incident names. That operational context comes from incident management agencies and analytic processing layered on top of detections.

**What turns fire detections into wildfire intelligence?** Correlating related detections across space and time into a single incident, tracking growth, adding official agency reporting, and assessing exposure — which facilities, people, and assets sit in and near the fire's footprint.

## Wildfire Intelligence Starts with NASA FIRMS

NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) has become one of the world's most important sources of near real-time wildfire detection. Using thermal anomaly observations from MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors, FIRMS identifies active fires across the globe, often within hours of satellite overpass, providing one of the earliest indications that a wildfire may be burning.

For organizations operating globally, FIRMS provides tremendous value:

  * Near real-time wildfire detection
  * Global geographic coverage
  * Consistent satellite observations
  * Frequent updates
  * Open, authoritative data



At DisasterAWARE, NASA FIRMS serves as one of the foundational inputs into our wildfire intelligence pipeline. But raw satellite detections alone rarely answer the questions organizations actually need answered.

## The Challenge with Raw Fire Detections

A thermal hotspot isn't the same thing as a wildfire. A single wildfire may generate hundreds — or thousands — of satellite detections over time. Likewise:

  * Multiple satellites observe the same fire
  * Detections arrive at different times
  * Clouds and smoke affect observations
  * Hotspots don't describe fire behavior
  * Hotspots don't define fire perimeters
  * Hotspots don't indicate incident names
  * Hotspots don't identify containment status



For an operations center, insurance carrier, emergency manager, or corporate security team, thousands of individual thermal anomalies are difficult to operationalize.

The real question isn't _"Where are the hotspots?"_ It's _"What wildfire is threatening my people or assets?"_

# DisasterAWARE Expands European Severe Weather Intelligence with MeteoAlarm Integration

**Published**: 2026-08-10  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/meteoalarm-integration-european-severe-weather-alerts  
**Summary**: DisasterAWARE now integrates MeteoAlarm: official severe weather warnings from 38 European national weather services, unified with global multi-hazard intelligence, exposure assessment, and alerting in one operational picture.

**Organizations operating across Europe can now access authoritative regional severe weather alerts alongside DisasterAWARE's global multi-hazard intelligence platform.**

As severe weather becomes more frequent and disruptive across Europe, organizations are under increasing pressure to detect threats earlier, understand potential impacts faster, and coordinate response across multiple countries.

Today we're excited to announce that DisasterAWARE now integrates MeteoAlarm, Europe's official multi-national severe weather warning system, significantly expanding our European weather intelligence capabilities.

The integration provides customers with trusted government-issued severe weather alerts from 38 European countries, seamlessly combined with DisasterAWARE's existing global [event intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/what-is-event-intelligence>) platform.

## Why European Severe Weather Monitoring Is Different

Monitoring severe weather across Europe presents unique challenges.

Unlike the United States, where organizations often rely on a single national weather authority, Europe consists of dozens of national meteorological agencies, each issuing warnings using different formats, terminology, severity scales, and update schedules.

For multinational insurers, supply chain operators, logistics providers, financial institutions, governments, and critical infrastructure organizations, monitoring weather risk often means stitching together information from many different sources.

That complexity slows decision making. DisasterAWARE simplifies this by bringing authoritative alerts into a single operational picture.

## What Is MeteoAlarm?

MeteoAlarm is Europe's official severe weather early-warning dissemination system, operated by EUMETNET — the network of European National Meteorological and Hydrological Services — and aggregating awareness information from 38 of those national services.

Rather than generating its own forecasts, MeteoAlarm aggregates official warnings issued directly by participating national meteorological agencies.

Warnings include hazards such as:

  * Severe thunderstorms
  * Heavy rainfall
  * Flood-producing precipitation
  * High winds
  * Snow and ice
  * Extreme temperatures
  * Coastal hazards
  * Fog
  * Avalanche conditions



Each alert includes official warning levels, affected regions, timing, and hazard descriptions directly from participating national weather agencies.

## One Platform for Global Hazard Intelligence

The MeteoAlarm integration strengthens DisasterAWARE's mission of delivering the world's most comprehensive operational hazard intelligence platform.

Organizations no longer need separate monitoring tools for different regions. Instead, DisasterAWARE provides unified monitoring across severe weather, tropical cyclones, flooding, wildfires, earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanoes, drought, air quality, civil unrest, maritime hazards, industrial accidents, and hundreds of additional hazard intelligence layers.

Customers receive a consistent operational experience regardless of where an event occurs.

_DisasterAWARE Enterprise on August 10, 2026: European severe weather, extreme temperature, wind, and marine warnings — sourced from national meteorological services via the MeteoAlarm integration — alongside the platform's global hazard picture. Coverage density across Europe is substantially higher than before the integration._
